segments.text: Shine a laser through a tiny slide with the letter F on it.
On a far wall, you don't see an F. You see streaks and fringes.
That pattern is the Fourier transform of the F, computed by the light itself.
Put a lens right behind the slide, and the same pattern appears just one focal length away.
Why does light compute Fourier transforms, for free?
Remember episode one: any field is a sum of plane waves, each heading in its own direction, sin θ = kx/k.
Their amplitudes form the field's spectrum: its Fourier transform.
Up close behind a slit, the waves still overlap, and you mostly see a shadow.
Now step back, a thousand times farther.
Each plane wave travels in a straight line. So far away, the directions come apart: direction θ lands at x = z tan θ.
So the pattern on the wall is the spectrum itself, spread out in space. This is Fraunhofer diffraction.
How far is far? The pattern grows like zλ/D, and it must dwarf the slit width D: z ≫ D²/λ.
But why a Fourier transform? Follow the light from a point x′ on the slide to a point x on the wall.
For small angles, the path length is nearly a parabola: z + (x − x′)²/2z.
The wall adds up waves from every point of the slide, each with phase k times that path.
Expand the square. The x² term is a curved phase on the wall that brightness can't see.
The cross term is exactly the Fourier kernel: position x on the wall picks out the frequency kx = k·x/z.
The x′² term is a chirp across the slide: its wiggles speed up toward the edges. Far away it flattens to one, leaving a pure Fourier transform.
Closer in, the chirp scrambles it. Could we cancel it?
A lens is glass that's thicker in the middle, so it delays the centre most. That's a phase e^(−ikx²/2f): an opposite chirp.
Watch a flat wave pass through. It leaves curved, and converges to a point one focal length f behind the lens.
Tilt the wave, and the focus slides sideways, to x = f tan θ.
Three directions, three separate spots. A lens sorts light by direction.
A slit sends out a whole spectrum of directions, so its spectrum appears in the focal plane, not at infinity.
In the math, the lens's chirp exactly cancels the slide's chirp when z = f.
Move the slide one focal length in front of the lens, and even the curved phase vanishes: an exact Fourier transform.
Now add a second lens, one more focal length on. It transforms the spectrum again, and the picture comes back.
Upside down! Two Fourier transforms don't undo each other: they mirror x into −x.
This is the 4f system. The middle plane holds the spectrum, sorted by direction, so a mask there edits it, frequency by frequency.
A pinhole keeps only the low frequencies, and the image blurs.
A small dot that blocks the centre keeps only the high frequencies, so just the edges survive.
Now a harder case: a living cell. It's nearly transparent; it only delays the light a little.
At each point, the light is a big arrow plus a tiny one at 90°, so its length barely changes. The camera sees nothing.
The big arrow is light that went straight through, and the first lens focuses it all into the central spot.
So delay just that spot by a quarter wave.
Now the arrows line up, and the cell appears.
That's Frits Zernike's phase contrast microscope, the 1953 Nobel Prize.
On a computer, you can choose from three propagators.
The angular spectrum method from episode one: FFT, multiply, inverse FFT. Exact, on the same grid as the input, and best up close.
Single-FFT Fresnel: multiply by the chirp, then one FFT. The output grid stretches with distance, Δx′ = λz/NΔx, so it's best far away.
And Fraunhofer: drop the chirp, and it's just one FFT.
The catch: chirps. Once a chirp's wiggles get shorter than two samples, the samples trace a false, slower wave: aliasing.
The angular spectrum chirp speeds up as z grows, while the Fresnel chirp slows down. They trade places at zc = NΔx²/λ: angular spectrum below it, Fresnel above.
Far away, or at a lens's focus, each direction lands on its own spot, so light lays out its own spectrum.
A second lens brings the picture back, with a mask in between to edit it.
Where it breaks: our shortcut assumed small angles. For steep ones, use the exact kz from episode one.
And a real lens is finite: it only catches directions up to some angle. That cutoff is why every image is blurry.
